item.title: [Update] AceVector IPO Subscribed 23% On Day 1, Retail Quota Booked 62%
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Update| September 25, 2026 18:55 IST Snapdeal parent AceVector’s ₹420 Cr IPO was subscribed 23% at the end of the…
item.content:encoded:
Update| September 25, 2026 18:55 IST

Snapdeal parent AceVector’s ₹420 Cr IPO was subscribed 23% at the end of the first day of bidding today. The issue received bids for 1.72 Cr shares against 7.42 Cr shares on offer, according to BSE data as of 17:00 IST.

The retail portion recorded the highest subscription rate at 62%, receiving bids for 85.74 Lakh shares against 1.37 Cr shares earmarked for the category.

Non-institutional investors (NIIs) bid for 86.70 Lakh shares against their allocation of 2.06 Cr shares, subscribing to 42% of their quota.

Within the NII category, the portion for bids above ₹2 Lakh and up to ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 71%, while the portion for bids above ₹10 Lakh was booked 28%.

Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) were yet to place bids for the 3.99 Cr shares reserved for them.

Original | September 25, 2026 14:37 IST

Snapdeal parent AceVector’s ₹420 Cr IPO was subscribed 9% as of 14:12 IST on the first day of bidding, with investors bidding for 65.11 Lakh shares against 7.42 Cr shares on offer, according to BSE data.

Retail investors led bidding, subscribing to 36% of their quota. They placed bids for 49.85 Lakh shares against 1.37 Cr shares reserved for them.

Non-institutional investors (NIIs) bid for 15.27 Lakh shares against their allocation of 2.06 Cr shares, subscribing to 7% of the portion.

Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) were yet to place bids against the 3.99 Cr shares earmarked for them.

The IPO will close on September 29 (Tuesday). AceVector has set a price band of ₹30-₹32 per share, valuing the company at up to ₹1,741.4 Cr ($181.7 Mn). Its shares are expected to list on the BSE and NSE on October 5.

The issue comprises a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an OFS of up to 4.16 Cr shares, worth ₹133 Cr at the upper end of the price band.

Ahead of the public issue, AceVector raised ₹189 Cr from anchor investors yesterday. Helios Mutual Fund and Taurus Ethical Fund were the only domestic mutual funds to participate, together picking up 93.75 Lakh shares, or 15.87% of the anchor allocation.

AceVector plans to use ₹132 Cr of the net proceeds from the fresh issue for Snapdeal’s marketing and business promotion, and another ₹50 Cr for its technology infrastructure. The remaining proceeds will go towards acquisitions and general corporate purposes.

Founded in 2010 by Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, Snapdeal once competed with Flipkart and Amazon before losing ground. Following the collapse of its proposed merger with Flipkart in 2017, it pivoted to a value-focused ecommerce model.

Besides Snapdeal, AceVector’s businesses include listed ecommerce enablement platform Unicommerce and consumer brands business Stellaro Brands. The group adopted the AceVector identity in 2022.

On the financial front, AceVector’s restated net loss narrowed nearly 64% to ₹45.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹126.3 Cr in FY25. Operating revenue rose 29.2% to ₹510.3 Cr from ₹395 Cr.

item.title: [Update] Moneyview IPO Subscribed 6.01X At End Of Day 2
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Update | September 25, 2026, 17:40 IST Moneyview’s IPO was subscribed 6.01X at the end of the second day of…
item.content:encoded:
Update | September 25, 2026, 17:40 IST

Moneyview’s IPO was subscribed 6.01X at the end of the second day of bidding, with investors placing bids for 139.8 Cr shares against 23.25 Cr shares on offer.

Non-institutional investors (NIIs) led demand, subscribing to their allotted quota 15.41X with bids for 77.41 Cr shares against 5.02 Cr shares on offer.

Within the NII category, the portion for bids exceeding ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 14.33X, while the segment for bids above ₹2 Lakh and up to ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 17.57X.

The retail portion was subscribed 5.18X, receiving bids for 60.74 Cr shares against 11.72 Cr shares on offer.

Meanwhile, qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) subscribed to 0.25X of their allotted quota, placing bids for 1.66 Cr shares against 6.51 Cr shares on offer.

Original | September 25, 2026, 13:15 IST

Digital lender Moneyview’s ₹1,092 Cr IPO was subscribed 3.55X by 13:15 IST on the second day of bidding. The public issue received bids for 82.65 Cr shares against 23.25 Cr shares on offer, according to BSE data.

Non-institutional investors (NIIs) led the demand, placing bids for 39.01 Cr shares against the 5.02 Cr shares reserved for them, translating into a subscription of 7.77X.  

Within the category, the portion reserved for investors bidding between ₹2 Lakh and ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 10.08X. Meanwhile, the portion for bids exceeding ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 6.61X.

Retail investors subscribed to their quota 3.67X, placing bids for 43.02 Cr shares against the 11.72 Cr shares reserved for them.

The qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) portion received bids for 61.45 Lakh shares against the 6.51 Cr shares reserved for the category, translating into a subscription of 0.09X. 

The issue ended the first day of bidding with a subscription of 1.44X. 

Moneyview has fixed the IPO price band at ₹32-₹34 per share. At the upper end of the price band, the IPO values the company at around ₹5,985 Cr ($624 Mn).

The public issue comprises a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹750 Cr and an OFS of up to 10.05 Cr shares, amounting to around ₹341.7 Cr at the upper end of the price band.

The IPO will close on September 28 (Monday), while the company’s shares are scheduled to list on the stock exchanges on October 1 (Thursday).

Ahead of the IPO, Moneyview raised ₹327.5 Cr from anchor investors by allotting 9.63 Cr equity shares at ₹34 apiece. Seven domestic mutual funds subscribed to 6.96 Cr shares worth around ₹236.7 Cr. Other anchor investors included Goldman Sachs, Amundi Funds, 360 ONE, HDFC Life Insurance Company, and India Acorn Fund.

Cofounders and promoters Puneet Agarwal and Sanjay Aggarwal, along with investors such as Accel, Tiger Global Management, Ribbit Capital, and DI Investment, are selling shares through the OFS. 

Moneyview intends to use ₹325 Cr of the fresh issue proceeds to support loan disbursals under default loss guarantee arrangements. Another ₹250 Cr will be infused into its NBFC subsidiary Whizdm Finance to augment its capital base, while the remaining proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes.

The lending tech company offers personal loans, payments, investments, and insurance through its digital platform.

On the financial front, Moneyview’s consolidated net profit jumped 2.6X to ₹173.8 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹67.2 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Its operating revenue rose 50.2% to ₹1,041.1 Cr from ₹693 Cr during the period.

For FY26, Moneyview’s operating revenue grew to ₹3,351.2 Cr from ₹2,339.1 Cr in FY25. Its consolidated profit increased marginally to ₹242.7 Cr from ₹240.3 Cr due to exceptional losses of ₹206.7 Cr.

item.title: GalaxEye Gets ₹63.8 Cr RDI Support For Multisensor Satellite Tech
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Spacetech startup GalaxEye has secured ₹63.84 Cr in financial support under the Centre’s Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund to…
item.content:encoded:
Spacetech startup GalaxEye has secured ₹63.84 Cr in financial support under the Centre’s Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund to develop its next-generation multisensor satellite technology.

The Technology Development Board (TDB), under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), has signed an agreement with the Bengaluru-based startup to provide the support through optionally convertible debentures.

The project has a total approved cost of ₹247.69 Cr, the Centre said in a statement. It aims to develop an indigenous satellite capable of OptoSAR imaging at a resolution finer than 0.5 metres. The project will take the technology from Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 6 to TRL 9, progressing from a demonstrated prototype towards a system proven in operation.

GalaxEye’s technology combines synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and electro-optical (EO) imaging. While optical imaging can be affected by cloud cover and lighting conditions, SAR can capture images through clouds and without daylight. By combining the two, the startup aims to provide high-resolution Earth observation across different weather and lighting conditions.

The proposed satellite’s applications include wide-area and long-range surveillance, detection of people and vehicles, and target classification, the government said.

“The agreement with GalaxEye reflects TDB’s focus on enabling indigenous capabilities in emerging space technologies and supporting their journey towards commercialisation,” TDB secretary Rajesh Kumar Pathak said.

GalaxEye Builds Its Satellite Capabilities 

Founded in 2021 by Suyash Singh, Denil Chawda, Kishan Thakkar, Pranit Mehta, and Rakshit Bhatt, GalaxEye builds multi-sensor earth observation satellites designed to provide high-resolution imaging and geospatial intelligence catering to sectors such as defence, agriculture, infrastructure and disaster management. 

The startup raised ₹44.2 Cr as part of an ongoing Series A round earlier this year, with investors including Speciale Invest, Rainmatter, MV Core and Mounttech Growth Fund. The IIT Madras-incubated startup has raised nearly $27 Mn in funding to date from investors like Speciale Invest, Mela Ventures, and Anicut Capital.

The startup claims to be building the world’s first multi-sensor earth observation satellite and aims to deploy a constellation of indigenous micro-satellites with data fusion capabilities. 

Earlier this month, GalaxEye received a US patent for satellite imaging technology, the first of its kind for an Indian spacetech startup. The patent covers the core architecture behind the startup’s proprietary OptoSAR technology. 

This came after the startup launched its maiden OptoSAR satellite under ‘Mission Drishti’ in May, which was touted as India’s largest privately built earth observation satellite and the world’s first imaging satellite using OptoSAR. However, it lost communication with the satellite in July due to an anomaly linked to a geomagnetic solar storm. 

The startup is now targeting the launch of two new OptoSAR satellites in the next two years while expanding its in-house capabilities to further strengthen quality, reliability, and execution.

Spacetech Funding Enters New Phase

The agreement adds to support for spacetech startups under the Centre’s ₹1 Lakh Cr RDI Fund, approved in July 2025 to increase private-sector participation in research, development, and innovation.

The fund is designed to finance technology development and commercialisation through long-term capital. It operates through a two-tier structure, with the Anusandhan National Research Foundation acting as the first-level custodian and institutions such as TDB and the Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council serving as second-level fund managers.

According to the government statement, TDB has approved 22 projects with a combined project cost of ₹4,744 Cr, involving ₹2,192 Cr in RDI support.

GalaxEye joins other spacetech startups backed under the programme. In May, Dhruva Space secured ₹105 Cr for Project Garud, which aims to develop a standardised satellite platform for large-scale deployments across telecom, earth observation, and national security applications.

The public funding comes alongside larger private investments in the sector. Indian spacetech startups have raised nearly $250 Mn in 2026 so far. These include Skyroot Aerospace’s $60 Mn round, which made it India’s first spacetech unicorn, and Pixxel’s $100 Mn Series C to expand satellite manufacturing and imaging capabilities.

item.title: How Enterprises Are Building Robust Infra Backbone For AI At Scale
item.dc:creator: Inc42 BrandLabs
item.description: After the proliferation of AI adoption, enterprise India has started to ask whether its infrastructure is robust enough to survive…
item.content:encoded:
After the proliferation of AI adoption, enterprise India has started to ask whether its infrastructure is robust enough to survive the shift. With the country’s enterprise AI market expected to cross $71 Bn by 2030, boardroom mandates around AI are accelerating, cloud costs are spiralling, data pipelines are buckling under the weight of unstructured inputs, and CTOs are discovering that pilots that worked in isolation can collapse the moment they are pushed into production at scale.

Therefore, enterprises across sectors are moving beyond productivity tools into core product development and delivery processes, including coding copilots, automated testing, and AI-driven IT service management. 

As a result, the conversation and its implementation are now shifting from experimentation to predictability, governance and cost control.

To unpack this shift, India’s leading tech voices joined Inc42 and Oracle for CTO Dialogues, featuring a roundtable on ‘Building The Infrastructure Backbone For AI At Scale’, followed by a fireside chat and a session exploring where enterprise AI strategies often fall short.

The roundtable was moderated by Sameer Dhanrajani, CEO of 3AI and AIQRATE, and featured the following speakers:

  • Ankit Mehra, cofounder and CEO, GyanDhan
  • Mashiyat Hussain, engineering lead, Backend, HYPD
  • Nitish Gupta, SVP – technology, NimbusPost
  • Sanjeev Singh, VP engineering, DeHaat
  • Shubhanshu Chouhan, CTO, Pidge
  • Vivek Gupta, senior director and head of technology cloud sales at Oracle India

Building A Robust Infra Backbone For AI 

The roundtable, moderated by Dhanrajani, addressed the harder question of how enterprises actually operationalise AI at scale, with six leaders spanning cloud, fintech, D2C, agritech, logistics and last-mile delivery.

Oracle India’s Vivek Gupta opened the conversation by arguing that enterprises chasing AI at scale are often solving for the wrong constraint. 

“AI at scale is not a GPU problem… It’s an engineering problem that needs to be solved,” said Gupta. 

According to Gupta, the bottleneck for many companies when implementing AI is not compute availability, but the ability to define a clear business outcome before they begin building. That focus on the problem itself resonated with GyanDhan’s Ankit Mehra, who pushed back against the instinct to reach for AI as a default fix. 

Having run workloads at his own company for testing purposes, Mehra said he had seen more problems traced to poorly framed questions than to actual scale limitations.

“Really solve for the problem that you’re trying to solve rather than just running with the hype part of it,” Mehra added.

But even when the problem is clearly defined, the data feeding these systems can present a different set of challenges. 

HYPD’s Hussain brought the conversation to data itself, describing the unpredictability of user-generated content on a creator platform, with comments arriving from varied regions and formats and no consistent pattern to model against.

“Data variety is a major problem for us. We cannot always predict what kind of data we will receive. For example, on our platform, creators receive comments from people across different regions and backgrounds, making it difficult to predict the nature and variety of the data,” said Hussain.

That unpredictability becomes even more complex when AI is layered on top of existing data challenges, and the VP of engineering at DeHaat, Singh, reiterated the same. According to Singh, the nature of the problem has shifted over the past decade, from a pure data-management challenge to a compounded one.

“Earlier it was only a data problem, shuffling of data, creating or churning our money. Now it’s a data-plus-AI problem. So, we have faced both,” said Singh.

For businesses operating at scale, however, identifying the problem and managing the data is only part of the equation. The infrastructure itself has to be tailored to the use case. 

The SVP of technology at NimbusPost, Gupta, grounded the discussion in logistics, where infrastructure decisions vary sharply by use case and margin. Getting the right setup, he said, comes only through costly trial and error.

“The right choice would come out of experimentation, and that experimentation would need a good amount of money… infrastructure is something wherein different industries would have different use cases,” he said. 

And that experimentation becomes even harder when AI is deployed in live operational environments, where a wrong decision can directly affect costs and performance. 

Chouhan, CTO of Pidge, concluded on a note of caution around automation in last-mile operations. Rider and delivery allocation, he said, still cannot be handed fully to opaque models.

“We cannot rely on an ambiguous, black-box algorithm like AI to always make the right decision. If we put AI in that place, our costs will go up, and we cannot guarantee performance,” said Chouhan.

Hidden Costs And Risks Of Scaling AI

The conversation then moved from the roundtable to a fireside chat, where the focus shifted from the broader challenges of building AI infrastructure to the risks enterprises face as they scale these deployments from pilots.

Dhanrajani, also moderating the fireside, opened the AI infrastructure conversation by pressing his two panellists, Ankit Gupta, CTO of Policybazaar for Business, and Nitin Kaushik, director of technology, Cloud Engineering, at Oracle, on where enterprise AI strategies tend to break down first.

Building AI capability, Gupta argued, is not only an infrastructure and use-case problem. According to him, it is also a trust challenge that many organisations underestimate. He noted that, without the right controls, prompts and AI-agent interactions can create pathways to expose sensitive enterprise information.

“Earlier we used to say, it is garbage in, garbage out, but today, the risk is that poorly governed inputs can lead to sensitive information getting out. That is why security, data governance, identity, and access controls must be designed into AI systems from the start,” Gupta said. 

Oracle’s Kaushik picked up the thread when the conversation turned to cost, an issue Dhanrajani termed as the “elephant in the room” for most enterprises deep into their AI rollouts. 

Token consumption, Kaushik said, is rising in ways many organisations are not prepared for. “I have met customers that are consuming trillions of tokens a day. We hear cases where organisations say their AI bills are beginning to approach – or even exceed – the value they associate with the business impact they are receiving.” 

Infra Gap Behind AI Deployment

Kaushik followed the fireside chat with a deeper look at why AI deployments break down after the pilot stage. According to Oracle’s director of cloud engineering, companies face three recurring challenges behind AI implementation. 

Cloud costs are often unpredictable, and data silos can create multiple versions of the same dataset – undermining the consistency and reliability of AI outputs. At the same time, cloud infrastructure has traditionally been built to prioritise availability over performance. 

According to him, Oracle rebuilt from the infrastructure layer up with dedicated compute and memory, off-box virtualisation to reduce network load on the CPU, and RDMA-based networking designed to deliver low-latency communication across GPU clusters.

Taken together, the roundtable and fireside chat pointed to a common thread: enterprise AI’s biggest constraints are not just computational, but organisational. Enterprises are grappling with engineering discipline, data governance, cost visibility and trust, rather than mere GPU access.

Tech leaders across the sessions converged on the same view that these factors, alongside access to compute, will ultimately determine whether an AI deployment survives the move from pilot to production.

The post How Enterprises Are Building Robust Infra Backbone For AI At Scale appeared first on Inc42 Media.

item.title: Dextr AI Raises $6.7 Mn To Build AI Agents For Hospitality Industry
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Hospitality-focused AI startup Dextr AI has raised $6.7 Mn (about ₹64.2 Cr) in a seed funding round led by Elevation…
item.content:encoded:
Hospitality-focused AI startup Dextr AI has raised $6.7 Mn (about ₹64.2 Cr) in a seed funding round led by Elevation Capital, with participation from Foundation Capital.

The startup plans to deploy the fresh capital towards product development, team expansion, and scaling its AI deployments across global hospitality markets, including India.

Founded in 2025 by Sajid Shariff and Scott Arnold, Dextr AI builds specialised AI agents for hospitality businesses. Its platform automates tasks across reservations, guest management, back-office operations, staffing, sales, and marketing.

Dextr said it serves hundreds of properties across the US, Canada, the UK, and other European markets, including franchised properties operating under brands such as Hilton, Wyndham, Best Western, and IHG.

The startup claims to process more than 1 Mn interactions every month. It also said its platform collects payments through voice-based reservations, processing tens of millions of dollars monthly on behalf of customers.

As part of its India expansion plans, Dextr is targeting operational gaps such as missed calls, unanswered enquiries, staffing shortages, and unattended guest requests.

Dextr follows what it calls a “forward-deployed” model, under which its AI strategists and engineers work directly with hospitality businesses to identify tasks for automation and integrate its agents into their operations.

Its Daisy agent handles voice-based reservations, booking changes, and upselling in more than 90 languages. Alfred manages guest requests, complaints, and contactless check-ins, while Manny handles staff rostering, task allocation, productivity tracking, and potential overtime.

Another agent, Cosmo, supports direct bookings through AI-powered search, targeted marketing campaigns, and efforts to bring back past guests.

Dextr currently has a team of nearly 20 employees, spread across India and the US, including AI product builders, strategists and engineers. 

For Elevation, Dextr is another investment in startups automating customer interactions and business workflows. In October last year, the investor led GreyLabs AI’s ₹85 Cr Series A round, which also saw participation from Z47 and angel investors. GreyLabs focuses on financial institutions, offering voice agents and speech analytics to automate contact centre operations.

Elevation also led a $6 Mn funding round in Adopt AI, which helps users automate software workflows through text commands. These investments span both industry-specific applications, such as hospitality and financial services, and tools designed to automate workflows across businesses.

item.title: Rivet Bags $10.5 Mn From Peak XV, Others To Scale Dating Platform In US
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Dating startup Rivet has raised $10.5 Mn (about ₹100.6 Cr) in seed funding from Peak XV Partners, Shine Capital, and…
item.content:encoded:
Dating startup Rivet has raised $10.5 Mn (about ₹100.6 Cr) in seed funding from Peak XV Partners, Shine Capital, and Blume Ventures to build and scale its community-driven matchmaking platform.

The startup plans to use the fresh capital to develop its product, expand distribution, and scale across the US. It announced its nationwide US launch yesterday.

Besides US, Rivet has an office in Delhi NCR, with its engineering and machine learning teams largely based in India.

Founded in 2025 by former Tinder and Match Group executive Taru Kapoor and Rajat Sahni, who previously served as CEO of CarDekho’s used-car business, Rivet offers a dating platform built around community recommendations.

The startup calls its model “social matching”. Users can join as “matchers” to assess potential pairs and recommend introductions they think would work.

These recommendations contribute to a social matching score for each potential pair. Pairs with high scores are introduced to each other, after which both individuals independently decide whether to connect and begin a conversation.

People who are not looking to date can also join solely as matchers. The startup describes its model as a “give-to-get” approach, allowing users to help others find connections while receiving recommendations for themselves.

The startup also counts former Tinder and OkCupid CEO Elie Seidman among its early investors. Seidman advised and mentored Kapoor during Rivet’s development.

The startup competes with dating and matchmaking platforms such as Tinder, Hinge, Bumble, The League, and Wingman. Its community-driven approach makes participation by people willing to recommend matches an important part of its expansion, alongside attracting singles seeking connections.

Rivet’s pitch centres on addressing the frustration of browsing profiles without finding a connection. Kapoor argued that while dating apps expanded the pool of potential partners, they also made the experience feel transactional and isolating.

The startup is betting that recommendations from other people can help surface potential matches that users might otherwise dismiss on swipe-based apps.

item.title: How Astrobase Is Building The Base For Tomorrow’s Medium-Lift Rockets
item.dc:creator: Shraddha Goled
item.description: In June 2026, three spacetech startups became the first cohort to receive funds selected under the Indian National Space Promotion…
item.content:encoded:
In June 2026, three spacetech startups became the first cohort to receive funds selected under the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre’s (IN-SPACe) Technology Adoption Fund’s (TAF) ₹500 Cr scheme. Bengaluru-based Astrobase Technologies was selected along with SatSure Analytics and TakeMe2Space, and got the backing despite being just two years old at the time. 

For Neeraj Khandelwal and Devakumar Thammisetty, founders of Astrobase, this milestone was a vindication of their passion for space tech. Classmates at IIT Bombay, the duo’s career paths diverged soon after graduation, before converging for Astrobase.  

Thammisetty spent 13 years at ISRO, where he worked on cryogenic engines. He also contributed significantly to CE-20, India’s only cryogenic engine. 

On the other hand, Khandelwal took the entrepreneurship route, and cofounded cryptocurrency exchange CoinDCX in 2018. 

Khandelwal told Inc42 he had actually considered entering the space sector when he started CoinDCX in 2018. However, private companies did not have the same opening into the sector at the time. 

To be sure, the ‘space’ for the private sector opened up in 2020 and private companies were able to access the facilities and services of ISRO, via the establishment of IN-SPACe, which acts as a single-window regulator-facilitator.
